subject: English
topic: Sentence Correction & Common Errors (60 Master Sets)
exam_tips: Common errors in written exams test Subject-Verb Agreement, Pronoun Cases, Prepositional idioms, Parallelism, and Uncountable Nouns.

items.incorrect: He is senior than me.
items.correct: He is senior to me.
items.rule: Latin adjectives ending in -ior (senior, junior, prior, superior, inferior) take 'to', not 'than'.

items.incorrect: One of the boy is absent today.
items.correct: One of the boys is absent today.
items.rule: 'One of the' is always followed by a plural noun and a singular verb.

items.incorrect: He gave me an advice.
items.correct: He gave me a piece of advice. (or: some advice)
items.rule: 'Advice' is an uncountable noun and cannot be preceded directly by 'a' or 'an'.

items.incorrect: I prefer reading than writing.
items.correct: I prefer reading to writing.
items.rule: 'Prefer' takes the preposition 'to' when comparing two actions or things.

items.incorrect: The sceneries of Cox's Bazar are charming.
items.correct: The scenery of Cox's Bazar is charming.
items.rule: 'Scenery' is uncountable; it has no plural form 'sceneries'.

items.incorrect: Neither Rahim nor his friends was present.
items.correct: Neither Rahim nor his friends were present.
items.rule: In 'Neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (friends -> were).

items.incorrect: Each of the students have done their homework.
items.correct: Each of the students has done his/her homework.
items.rule: 'Each of' takes a singular verb and singular pronoun.

items.incorrect: He died from cancer.
items.correct: He died of cancer.
items.rule: When someone dies of a disease, the preposition 'of' is used (died of malaria/cancer).

items.incorrect: I, you and he are friends.
items.correct: You, he and I are friends.
items.rule: In normal statements, pronouns follow the 2nd, 3rd, 1st person order (2-3-1 rule).

items.incorrect: You, he and I are guilty.
items.correct: I, you and he are guilty.
items.rule: When confessing a mistake or guilt, the order is 1st, 2nd, 3rd person (1-2-3 rule).

items.incorrect: The news are true.
items.correct: The news is true.
items.rule: 'News' looks plural but takes a singular verb.

items.incorrect: Fifty miles are a long distance.
items.correct: Fifty miles is a long distance.
items.rule: Units of measurement, distance, time, and money take singular verbs when considered as a whole.

items.incorrect: He is good in English.
items.correct: He is good at English.
items.rule: 'Good at' means skilled or proficient in a subject.

items.incorrect: I saw a dream last night.
items.correct: I had a dream last night. (or: dreamt a dream)
items.rule: You do not 'see' a dream in English; you 'have' or 'dream' a dream.

items.incorrect: He prevented me to go there.
items.correct: He prevented me from going there.
items.rule: 'Prevent' takes 'from + verb-ing', not the infinitive 'to go'.

items.incorrect: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
items.correct: Unless you work hard, you will fail.
items.rule: 'Unless' is already negative; do not use 'not' inside an unless-clause.

items.incorrect: He insisted me to go.
items.correct: He insisted on my going.
items.rule: 'Insist' takes the preposition 'on' followed by a gerund with a possessive pronoun.

items.incorrect: The patient died before the doctor came.
items.correct: The patient had died before the doctor came.
items.rule: In past perfect with 'before', the earlier action takes 'had + past participle'.

items.incorrect: He discussed about the matter.
items.correct: He discussed the matter.
items.rule: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb; it does not take the preposition 'about'.

items.incorrect: I look forward to hear from you.
items.correct: I look forward to hearing from you.
items.rule: 'Look forward to' is followed by a gerund (verb+ing).

items.incorrect: He came here with a view to learn English.
items.correct: He came here with a view to learning English.
items.rule: 'With a view to' is always followed by a gerund (V-ing).

items.incorrect: Do you know who did break the glass?
items.correct: Do you know who broke the glass?
items.rule: In indirect questions, auxiliary 'did' is not used.

items.incorrect: He is suffering from fever since Monday.
items.correct: He has been suffering from fever since Monday.
items.rule: An action starting in the past and continuing takes Present Perfect Continuous tense.

items.incorrect: I reached to the station in time.
items.correct: I reached the station in time.
items.rule: 'Reach' takes a direct object without the preposition 'to'.

items.incorrect: He is very weak that he cannot walk.
items.correct: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
items.rule: The correlative conjunction is 'so... that', not 'very... that'.

items.incorrect: No sooner did the bell ring when the students entered.
items.correct: No sooner did the bell ring than the students entered.
items.rule: 'No sooner... than' is the correct correlative pair.

items.incorrect: Hardly had I arrived than it began to rain.
items.correct: Hardly had I arrived when it began to rain.
items.rule: 'Hardly had... when' is the correct correlative pair.

items.incorrect: He told that he was ill.
items.correct: He said that he was ill. (or: He told me that he was ill)
items.rule: 'Tell' requires a personal object (told me), while 'say' does not.

items.incorrect: He is addict to gambling.
items.correct: He is addicted to gambling.
items.rule: 'Addicted to' is the correct adjective form meaning dependent on a bad habit.

items.incorrect: All that glitters are not gold.
items.correct: All that glitters is not gold.
items.rule: Proverb: 'All that glitters is not gold' takes a singular verb.

items.incorrect: He is taller between the two boys.
items.correct: He is the taller of the two boys.
items.rule: When comparing two specific items with 'of the two', use 'the + comparative'.

items.incorrect: I forbade him not to go.
items.correct: I forbade him to go.
items.rule: 'Forbid' is inherently negative; do not add 'not' after it.

items.incorrect: He is superior than all of us.
items.correct: He is superior to all of us.
items.rule: 'Superior' takes 'to', never 'than'.

items.incorrect: The climate of Sylhet is better than Dhaka.
items.correct: The climate of Sylhet is better than that of Dhaka.
items.rule: Comparisons must compare similar things: climate with climate ('that of Dhaka').

items.incorrect: I have no money in my pocket.
items.correct: I have no money with me. (or: I have no money in hand)
items.rule: Proper idiomatic English expression for having cash.

items.incorrect: He resigned from his post.
items.correct: He resigned his post.
items.rule: 'Resign' directly takes the post as its object without 'from'.

items.incorrect: What is the time in your watch?
items.correct: What is the time by your watch?
items.rule: The correct preposition for checking time with a watch is 'by'.

items.incorrect: He entered into the room.
items.correct: He entered the room.
items.rule: For physical entry, 'enter' does not take 'into'. ('Enter into' is only used for agreements).

items.incorrect: I am looking for a work.
items.correct: I am looking for a job. (or: looking for work)
items.rule: 'Work' is uncountable; use 'job' if using the article 'a'.

items.incorrect: Both of them did not come.
items.correct: Neither of them came.
items.rule: To express negative for both, use 'Neither of them came' instead of 'Both did not'.
